action: Prepare the field before the rains
title: Get the field ready early
farmer_summary: Clearing and ridging before the rains lets you plant as soon as the soil is wet.
still_to_find: Evidence that early land preparation helps farmers plant on time in Malawi.

action: Wait until the soil is wet a hand deep
title: Wait for enough moisture
farmer_summary: Seed planted in dry soil can fail to come up if the rain stops again.
still_to_find: Local guidance on how much rain or soil moisture is needed before planting.

action: Plant within a week of the first good rains
title: Plant with the first good rains
farmer_summary: Maize planted when the soil is wet after the first good rains uses the whole rainy season. Planting late shortens the season.
still_to_find: Yield lost per week of late planting in Malawi trials.

action: Put basal fertilizer in at planting
title: How much fertilizer for maize
farmer_summary: Most advice is a basal fertilizer at planting and urea top-dressing a few weeks later.
still_to_find: Malawi recommended rates per acre and the yield response at each rate.

action: Top-dress with urea a few weeks later
title: Top-dress when the crop grows fast
farmer_summary: Urea given a few weeks after planting feeds the crop when it needs nitrogen most.
still_to_find: Recommended timing of top-dressing, in weeks after planting.

action: Place it near the plant and cover it
title: Put fertilizer where the roots are
farmer_summary: Fertilizer placed close to the plant and covered with soil is used better and washes away less.
still_to_find: Placement method recommended in Malawi and its effect on yield.

action: Buy certified seed from an agro-dealer
title: Hybrid seed and local seed
farmer_summary: Hybrid seed usually yields more than local seed, but it must be bought new each season.
still_to_find: Yield difference on farmers' fields, and what happens with recycled hybrid seed.

action: Don't replant seed saved from a hybrid crop
title: Don't replant hybrid seed
farmer_summary: Seed saved from a hybrid crop gives a weaker crop the next season.
still_to_find: Yield of recycled hybrid seed compared with fresh seed.

action: Compare the seed price with the extra bags
title: Compare cost and benefit
farmer_summary: Hybrid seed costs more, so it pays when the extra harvest is worth more than the seed.
still_to_find: Hybrid seed price and typical extra yield, to estimate the payoff.

action: Add compost or manure before planting
title: Compost and manure
farmer_summary: Compost and animal manure add nutrients and help the soil hold water.
still_to_find: Yield effect alone and when combined with a smaller amount of fertilizer.

action: Leave crop residue on the field
title: Keep crop residue on the field
farmer_summary: Leaving maize stalks and leaves on the field adds organic matter and protects the soil.
still_to_find: Effect of keeping residue on soil and yield in Malawi.

action: Ask for a soil test before using lime
title: Soil quality and harvest
farmer_summary: Poor or acidic soil limits how much of the fertilizer the crop can use.
still_to_find: How soil organic matter and pH relate to maize yield in Malawi, and the effect of lime.

action: Plant pigeon peas, beans or groundnuts between maize rows
title: Maize with legumes
farmer_summary: Growing pigeon peas, beans or groundnuts with maize gives a second harvest and can feed the soil.
still_to_find: Effect on maize bags per hectare and on total harvest from the field.

action: Expect a little less maize, plus a second crop
title: What to expect from mixing
farmer_summary: Mixed fields usually give a little less maize, plus a second crop to eat or sell.
still_to_find: Maize and legume yields in mixed fields compared with maize alone.

action: Rotate where you plant them next season
title: Rotate the legume
farmer_summary: Moving the legume to a different part of the field each season spreads the soil benefit.
still_to_find: Benefit of legume rotation for the next maize crop.

action: Cover the soil with crop residue
title: Keeping water in the soil
farmer_summary: Mulching, tied ridges and pit planting keep rain in the field during dry spells.
still_to_find: Yield effect in dry seasons and labour needed.

action: Build ridges with ties across the slope
title: Tied ridges
farmer_summary: Small earth ties across the ridges hold rainwater so it soaks in instead of running off.
still_to_find: Yield effect of tied ridges in dry seasons.

action: Dig planting pits on dry or sandy land
title: Planting pits
farmer_summary: Pits around the planting station collect water and manure where the roots grow.
still_to_find: Yield effect and labour of planting pits in Malawi.

action: Dry the grain until it cracks when bitten
title: Dry the grain well
farmer_summary: Grain stored wet goes mouldy. Dry it until it cracks when bitten.
still_to_find: Safe moisture level for stored maize.

action: Store it in a sealed (hermetic) bag
title: Storing maize safely
farmer_summary: Dry the grain well and store it in hermetic bags off the floor to reduce weevil losses.
still_to_find: Storage losses with and without hermetic bags.

action: Keep bags off the floor and away from walls
title: Store off the floor
farmer_summary: Bags on the floor or against walls take up damp and are easy for pests to reach.
still_to_find: Storage losses with and without raised storage.

action: Ask about Aflasafe 2 to 3 weeks before flowering
title: A good fungus that protects the crop
farmer_summary: Aflasafe puts harmless fungi in the field that crowd out the ones that make aflatoxin. It is registered in Malawi.
fun_fact: In trials in 11 Malawi districts, Aflasafe cut aflatoxin in maize by more than 80%.
still_to_find: Where farmers can buy Aflasafe in Malawi, price per acre, application rate.

action: Harvest as soon as the cobs are dry
title: Do not leave dry maize in the field
farmer_summary: Cobs left standing after they are dry pick up more mould and insects. Harvest when husks are dry like paper and cobs hang down.
still_to_find: Malawi evidence on aflatoxin increase with delayed harvest.

action: Dry on a tarpaulin or mat, never on bare ground
title: Keep cobs off the soil
farmer_summary: The mould that makes aflatoxin lives in soil. Dry maize on a tarpaulin, mat or raised rack, never on bare ground.
fun_fact: In southern Malawi, farmers who dried maize on tarpaulins cut aflatoxin by about a fifth.

action: Sort out mouldy, broken and discoloured grain
title: Sorting removes most of the poison
farmer_summary: Most aflatoxin sits in a few bad grains. Picking out mouldy, broken, shrivelled and discoloured grain removes much of it.
fun_fact: Sorting out bad grains alone can remove 40 to 80% of aflatoxin.

action: Dry the grain to about 13% moisture
title: Dry enough to store
farmer_summary: Mould grows in damp grain. Store maize at about 13% moisture. Salt test: shake grain with dry salt in a jar for 2 to 3 minutes. If the salt does not stick, it is dry enough.
fun_fact: A jar of dry salt can tell you if maize is dry enough to store.
still_to_find: Malawi recommended storage moisture and a validated salt test method.

action: Store in a sealed bag, off the floor
title: Sealed bags stop mould growing
farmer_summary: Hermetic bags such as PICS keep air out, so mould and weevils cannot grow. Keep bags off the floor.
fun_fact: In Kenya, maize in hermetic bags had about one third of the aflatoxin of normal bags after 8 months.
still_to_find: Malawi trial of hermetic storage and aflatoxin.

title: A hidden poison
farmer_summary: Aflatoxin is made by mould on maize and groundnuts. It causes liver cancer and is linked to stunting in young children.
fun_fact: About 500 million of the world's poorest people eat aflatoxin in their staple food every day.

title: Soaking does not make it safe
farmer_summary: Aflatoxin stays in maize through soaking and fermenting. Throw away mouldy grain instead of trying to clean it.
fun_fact: In one study, aflatoxin was still there after maize was soaked and fermented for days.
still_to_find: A source on whether cooking reduces aflatoxin (often said not to).

title: Not safe for animals either
farmer_summary: Aflatoxin in mouldy feed passes into cows' milk. Do not feed mouldy grain to animals.

title: Common in Malawi maize
farmer_summary: Aflatoxin is common in maize and groundnuts in Malawi, and it costs the country export income.
fun_fact: In one study in southern Malawi, almost half of maize samples had more aflatoxin than the 20 ppb safety level.
still_to_find: Malawi Bureau of Standards limit for aflatoxin in maize.
